intro: Your world-models map leads the week, with hyper-connections from the trending papers, the physics of forgetting, Sakamoto in December, and a room that becomes a camera. Pick anything, or nothing.

items.title: World models: a one-week map of the field
items.description: Your idea, as one week across the three main families of world models. Latent-dynamics models that agents plan in (World Models, Dreamer, MuZero). JEPA-style predictors that predict in embedding space (I-JEPA, V-JEPA 2). Generative and interactive video worlds (Sora, Cosmos, Genie 3, World Labs Atlas). A recent survey is the spine.
items.why: The word world model now covers very different things. A map helps you read new papers and see which family a claim belongs to.

explain.what: A world model is a learned model that predicts how an environment changes, often given an action. Agents can use it to imagine outcomes before acting.
explain.why: It is one of the most active areas this year. It links reinforcement learning, self-supervised learning, video generation and robotics.
explain.how: Encode observations into a state, learn a dynamics model that predicts the next state, then plan or train a policy inside the model. The families differ in what they predict: compact latents, embeddings, or full pixels.
components: an encoder from observations to state
a decoder or prediction target (pixels, latents or embeddings)
a way to use it: planning, policy learning or simulation
explain.limitations: Pixel-perfect video can still break physics. A recent benchmark finds open interactive world models let objects pass through obstacles. Evaluation is unsettled, and there is a live debate on whether visual quality says anything about usefulness for decisions.
explain.research_relevance: Useful for agents, robotics, evaluation and representation learning. Good questions: what is the right prediction target, and how do you test that a model understands dynamics rather than appearance?

steps: Read the taxonomy sections of the comprehensive survey and sketch its axes on one page
Read the World Models paper by Ha and Schmidhuber (the interactive article is short) and DreamerV3's method section. Note what the latent state is and how the agent learns inside it
Read the V-JEPA 2 abstract and planning section. Write down why predicting embeddings instead of pixels might help

Look at Genie 3 and World Labs Atlas. Atlas (World Labs, September 2026) is a blog-only release with no paper: it generates camera-controlled video, reconstructs 3D scenes from photos and simulates them
Sort ten models you know into the survey's taxonomy. Then read the Non-penetrating World Models abstract and name one failure each family would have

items.title: New in AI: rethinking the residual connection with hyper-connections
items.description: The residual stream has been fixed since ResNet. Hyper-connections widen it into several parallel streams with learned mixing. DeepSeek's mHC made this stable by keeping the mixing matrices doubly stochastic. This week's trending papers on cmHC and loom attention push the idea further.
items.why: Two of the week's most upvoted papers are about how information flows between layers. It is a rare change to a part of the transformer most people never question.

explain.what: A residual connection adds a layer's input to its output. Hyper-connections keep n copies of the residual stream and learn how to mix them at every layer.
explain.why: Plain residuals trade off gradient flow against representation collapse. Learned mixing can do better, but unconstrained mixing can blow up or vanish over many layers.
explain.how: mHC projects each mixing matrix onto the Birkhoff polytope, the set of doubly stochastic matrices, using Sinkhorn iterations. Products of such matrices stay bounded, so the signal neither explodes nor dies.
components: a doubly stochastic constraint via Sinkhorn
explain.limitations: Extra memory for n streams. cmHC reports a trade-off: too little mixing wastes the streams, too much mixing makes them all the same.
explain.research_relevance: A clean case of a geometric constraint making training stable. The same idea shows up in optimal transport and Markov chains.

steps: Read the Hyper-Connections abstract and its main figure. Draw one layer with n = 2 streams
Read the mHC method section. Find where Sinkhorn is used and why
Read the cmHC and loom attention abstracts from this week. Write one sentence on what each changes
Do the doubly stochastic exercise in Research practice to see the maths behind the stability

items.title: Why doubly stochastic mixing is stable: prove it, then build Sinkhorn
items.description: A small proof plus a 20-line implementation. Show that doubly stochastic matrices are closed under products and never increase the norm of a vector. Then write Sinkhorn-Knopp and watch what repeated mixing does.
items.why: This is the maths behind mHC, and the same tool behind entropic optimal transport. Proving and building it beats reading about it.
steps: Prove that the product of two doubly stochastic matrices is doubly stochastic
Prove that a doubly stochastic matrix has spectral norm at most 1
Write Sinkhorn-Knopp in NumPy: start from exp(M) for a random M and alternate row and column normalisation. Plot the error against iterations
Multiply 50 random doubly stochastic 4x4 matrices. What does the product converge to? Connect this to the over-mixing problem in cmHC
hints: For closure, use the all-ones vector 1. A matrix A is doubly stochastic when A1 = 1 and 1ᵀA = 1ᵀ, with non-negative entries.
For the norm, the Birkhoff-von Neumann theorem says A is a convex combination of permutation matrices. Each permutation has norm 1, and a norm is convex.
For the product, think of a Markov chain whose stationary distribution is uniform. Where does every row end up?

items.title: The Banach fixed-point theorem: why contractions always converge
items.subject: maths
items.description: If a map pulls every pair of points closer by a fixed factor, repeating it always lands on one unique point. This one theorem explains why value iteration in RL converges, why many iterative solvers work, and why Picard's method solves differential equations.
items.why: Analysis is a growth area for you, and this theorem shows up all over ML theory. It is also the geometric idea behind contraction in cmHC.
steps: Read the definitions of a metric space, a complete space and a contraction
Follow the proof: show the iterates form a Cauchy sequence, then use completeness
Prove that the Bellman operator is a γ-contraction in the max norm
Find one map that pulls points closer but is not a contraction, and see why it can fail

items.title: Landauer's principle: forgetting has a physical cost
items.subject: physics

cross_domain.connection: Erasing one bit must release at least kT ln 2 of heat. Physics puts a floor under the cost of forgetting, a fun mirror of the question of what it costs a model to truly forget.

items.description: Erasing one bit of information must dissipate at least kT ln 2 of heat. This resolved the puzzle of Maxwell's demon, and it was measured directly in 2012 with a single bead in a laser trap.
items.why: It is where information theory meets thermodynamics. It also changes how you think about the word forget.
steps: Read Bennett's notes, sections on Maxwell's demon and on why erasure, not measurement, costs energy
Read the 2012 experiment's abstract and look at how a bead in a double-well potential stores one bit
Compute kT ln 2 at room temperature in joules and in electronvolts
Try the Landauer question in this week's physics questions

items.title: Predictive processing: is the brain a world model?
items.subject: neuroscience

cross_domain.connection: Predictive processing says the brain constantly predicts its senses and learns from errors. It pairs directly with this week's world-models map and the JEPA idea of predicting in a latent space.

items.description: A major theory in cognitive science says perception is mostly prediction. The brain guesses what comes next and only passes up the errors. Andy Clark's 2013 paper is the classic overview.

items.title: Which takes longer to appear: HH or HT?
items.subject: probability
items.description: Toss a fair coin until you see two heads in a row (HH). Separately, toss until you see a head followed by a tail (HT). What is the expected number of tosses for each? Most people guess they are equal.
items.why: A classic that trains you to set up states and expectations instead of trusting intuition.
hints: Define states by the last toss that matters.
For HT, once you have an H you can never lose progress. For HH, a T sends you back to the start.
Write E = 1 + (average of the next states) for each state and solve.
items.solution: For HT: from the start you wait 2 tosses on average for an H, then 2 more for a T, so 4. For HH: let E be the start and E_H the state after one H. E = 1 + (E_H + E)/2 and E_H = 1 + E/2. Solving gives E = 6. HH takes longer because a failure throws away your progress.

items.title: Five points in a square: two must be close
items.subject: maths
items.description: Place any five points inside a unit square. Show that two of them are at most √2/2 apart.
items.why: The pigeonhole principle is a small tool that solves surprisingly hard problems. It is good practice in looking for the right boxes.
hints: Split the square into four equal pieces.
What is the longest distance inside one small square?
items.solution: Cut the square into four squares of side 1/2. With five points, one small square holds two of them. The largest distance inside a square of side 1/2 is its diagonal, √2/2.

items.title: The spinning skater: where does the extra energy come from?
items.subject: physics
items.description: A skater spins with arms out, then pulls them in so her moment of inertia halves. Her angular speed doubles. What happens to her kinetic energy, and where does the difference come from?
items.why: Conservation laws are the backbone of physics. This one has a twist that many people miss.
hints: Angular momentum L = Iω is conserved because there is no outside torque.
Pulling the arms in takes force along the arms. Is any work done?
items.solution: L stays the same, so KE = L²/(2I) doubles when I halves. The extra energy comes from the work her muscles do pulling the arms inward against the outward pull of the rotation.
items.source: Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. I, Ch. 18 (Rotation in two dimensions)

items.title: The minimum energy to erase a gigabyte
items.subject: physics
items.description: Using Landauer's bound, what is the least energy needed to erase 1 gigabyte at room temperature, 300 K? Compare it with the energy of lifting a grain of sand one millimetre.
items.why: A quick Fermi-style calculation that makes the knowledge topic on Landauer's principle concrete.
hints: Each bit costs at least kT ln 2, with k = 1.38 × 10⁻²³ J/K.
A grain of sand weighs about 10⁻⁶ kg.
items.solution: kT ln 2 at 300 K is about 2.9 × 10⁻²¹ J. Times 8 × 10⁹ bits gives about 2.3 × 10⁻¹¹ J. Lifting 10⁻⁶ kg by 10⁻³ m takes about 10⁻⁸ J, roughly a thousand times more. Real chips use far more than the Landauer bound.

items.title: The Mpemba effect: can hot water freeze faster than cold?

items.why: It is a true scientific mystery about something in your kitchen, and a story about taking a student's observation seriously.

items.title: Three follow-up questions before your own view
items.topic: active listening and asking better questions
items.description: In one real conversation this week, when someone tells you about something they care about, ask three follow-up questions before you share your own opinion or story.
items.why: Follow-up questions are one of the simplest ways to make someone feel heard. Holding back your view for a moment also shows you what you would have missed.
steps: Pick a relaxed conversation, a meal or a walk
Ask three follow-ups that build on their last answer, for example: what happened next, how did that feel, what surprised you
Only then share your view
Afterwards, note one thing you learned that you would not have heard otherwise
items.then: Notice whether the other person talked longer or more openly than usual.

items.title: Explain one idea from this week at three levels
items.description: Take one idea from this week, such as world models or Landauer's principle. Explain it to one real person in three sentences, then with one good analogy, then ask them to explain it back.
items.why: Explaining clearly is a research skill and a people skill. Their explanation back shows you exactly what landed.
steps: Write your three sentences first
Find one everyday analogy
Explain it to a friend or family member who is not in your field
Ask them to say it back in their own words and listen for gaps
items.then: Rewrite your three sentences using what you learned.

items.title: Turn a room into a camera obscura

cross_domain.connection: A dark room with a small hole projects an upside-down image of the world outside. Artists from the Renaissance onward used this effect, and some argue painters like Vermeer did too.

items.description: Black out a window on a sunny day, leave one small hole, and the street outside appears upside down on your wall, in colour and in motion. It takes some cardboard, tape and patience.
items.why: Something weird and beautiful that you can make in an afternoon. It shows the physics of every camera and every eye.
steps: Pick a room with a window facing a bright outdoor scene
Cover the window fully with cardboard or foil
Cut a hole about 1 cm wide and wait 10 minutes for your eyes to adapt
Try a smaller hole and compare sharpness and brightness

lessons.title: Introducing yourself: はじめまして and 〜です
lessons.explanation: A Japanese self-introduction has three parts. Start with はじめまして (nice to meet you, said the first time only). Give your name with 〜です (I am …). End with よろしくおねがいします, which asks for a good relationship. You can drop わたしは (I) because it is clear from context.
